gloss_terse: Be light, swift, trifling; in Piel, to curse; in Hifil, to lighten or dishonor; also to subside or shake
gloss_readable: A versatile root whose core image is lightness — whether physical, social, or moral. In the Qal it describes what is swift (Hab 1:8), what subsides like floodwaters (Gen 8:11), or what is held in low esteem (Job 40:4). The Piel develops the dominant biblical sense of pronouncing a curse — making someone 'light' in standing before God and community (Gen 12:3; Exod 21:17). The Hifil can go either direction: lightening a literal burden (1 Kgs 12:4) or treating a person as worthless (Isa 23:9). Arabic قَلَّ (be small, scanty) and Ethiopic ቀለለ (be light, easy) preserve the original physical core from which the moral and verbal senses radiate.

senses.1: The dominant Piel sense: pronouncing a curse that diminishes someone's standing or invokes harm. Uniformly rendered by Arabic لَعَنَ, Korean 저주하다, and Swahili -laani across 41 occurrences. The Piel intensification transforms 'being light' into 'making someone light' — that is, stripping away weight, honor, and blessing (Gen 12:3; Exod 21:17; Lev 19:14).
senses.2: Hifil causative: to make a load or obligation physically lighter. Arabic خَفَّفَ and Spanish aligerar confirm the concrete sense. Used in appeals to reduce oppressive labor (1 Kgs 12:4, 9–10) and in Jethro's counsel to Moses to delegate judicial burdens (Exod 18:22).
senses.3: Nifal: to be a light, easy, or trifling matter — something not weighty enough to be significant. Korean 쉽다 (easy) and Arabic هَيِّنٌ capture this evaluative tone. In 1 Sam 18:23 David protests that becoming the king's son-in-law is no trifling thing; in Prov 14:6 knowledge comes easily to the discerning.
senses.4: Qal stative describing physical swiftness or speed of movement. Arabic أَسْرَعُ (swifter) and Korean 빠르다 (fast) match precisely. Applied to Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1:23), to fleeting days (Job 7:6; 9:25), and to invading cavalry swifter than leopards (Hab 1:8).
senses.5: Qal: to be of little account, despised, or lightly esteemed — the social-evaluative dimension of lightness. Arabic حَقِيرٌ (contemptible) and Swahili kudharauliwa (despised) converge. Hagar despises Sarai (Gen 16:4–5); Eli's unfaithful sons will be lightly esteemed (1 Sam 2:30); Job confesses his insignificance (Job 40:4).
senses.6: Hifil used of treating a person as worthless or dishonoring them — the causative counterpart of sense 5. Arabic أَهَانَ (dishonor) and Swahili kudhalilisha confirm the active-agent nuance. Isaiah announces God will first dishonor the land of Zebulun and Naphtali (Isa 9:1); Ezekiel charges Jerusalem with dishonoring parents (Ezek 22:7).
senses.7: Nifal describing swiftness or lightness of movement — overlapping with sense 4 but in the Nifal reflexive-passive stem. Arabic خِفَّة (lightness, agility) and Swahili wepesi (swift) align. Jeremiah's accusation that the leaders healed the wound lightly (Jer 6:14; 8:11) carries the nuance of superficial, too-quick treatment.
senses.8: Pual passive: to be cursed or under a curse — the passive counterpart of sense 1. Arabic يُلْعَنُ and Swahili -laaniwa confirm passive voice. Job 24:18 describes the cursed portion of the wicked; Isa 65:20 envisions the sinner dying at a hundred being considered accursed.
senses.9: Qal: to subside, abate, or diminish — said of the floodwaters in Gen 8:8, 11. Arabic خَفَّتْ (lightened, abated) and Swahili yamepungua (decreased) match this concrete physical sense of something becoming less heavy or voluminous.
senses.10: A distinct Piel sense of shaking, brandishing, or whetting — connected to the Pilpel root קַלְקֵל and cognate Arabic قَلْقَلَ (shake). Korean 갈았다 (sharpened) captures the Eccl 10:10 usage; Ezek 21:21 describes the king of Babylon shaking arrows for divination.
senses.11: Likely a Pilpel or Hitpalpel form describing trembling or shaking of the earth. The single occurrence in Jer 4:24 (mountains trembling) connects to the vibratory semantics of sense 10 and cognate Ethiopic ቈልቈለ (vibrate). Spanish se estremecían (they trembled) confirms the seismic imagery.
senses.12: A Nifal reflexive in 2 Sam 6:22 where David declares he will make himself even more lightly esteemed — voluntarily embracing social diminishment in worship. This bridges the 'despised' sense (5) with deliberate self-lowering, a theological motif unique to this passage.

gloss_terse: Do, make, perform; also produce, cause, keep, spend time, commit, consider, or labor
gloss_readable: The most versatile action verb in the New Testament, appearing over 570 times with a semantic range stretching from concrete making to abstract performing. At its core, poieo means to do or make — but context shapes it into remarkably distinct senses: a tree produces fruit (Matt 7:17), a host makes a banquet (Luke 14:12), a traveler spends time in a city (Acts 20:3), or a believer keeps a festival (Heb 11:28). Arabic distinguishes between فَعَلَ (do/act) and صَنَعَ (make/construct) where Greek uses one word, revealing the breadth this single verb covers.

senses.1: The general-purpose sense covering nearly every kind of purposeful action — doing, acting, performing. Arabic فَعَلَ/يَفْعَلُ, Korean 하다/행하다, and virtually every target language use their most basic action verb here. With 473 occurrences it is the default: doing the will of God (Matt 6:1), doing miracles (Matt 9:28), or doing on the Sabbath (Matt 12:2).
senses.2: To make, construct, or create something — bringing an object or entity into existence. Arabic صَنَعَ (fabricate) and Korean 만들다 (make) distinguish this from mere doing. Jesus makes a whip (John 2:15), God makes a path straight (Matt 3:3), and a tree is made good by its fruit (Matt 12:33).
senses.3: To produce or bear fruit — agricultural and metaphorical productivity. Arabic أَثْمَرَ (bear fruit), Korean 맺다 (bear), and Swahili kuzaa (produce) all deploy specialized vocabulary here rather than generic 'do.' Central to Jesus's teaching: every good tree produces good fruit (Matt 7:17); repentance must produce fruit worthy of itself (Matt 3:8).
senses.4: Causative: to make someone or something become a certain way, to render or appoint. Arabic جَعَلَ and Korean 하게 하다 (cause to be) capture this factitive nuance. Jesus made twelve to be apostles (Mark 3:14); a mustard seed makes great branches (Mark 4:32); invitations cause a dinner to happen (Luke 14:12–13).
senses.5: To spend or pass a period of time in a location. Arabic قَضَى (spend time) and Korean 보내다 (send/spend) reflect a specialized temporal usage distant from the core 'do.' Paul spent time in Antioch (Acts 18:23), three months in Greece (Acts 20:3), and a night and day in the deep (2 Cor 11:25).
senses.6: To keep, observe, or celebrate a religious occasion or festival. Korean 지키다 (keep/observe) and Swahili kusherehekea (celebrate) highlight the ritual dimension. Jesus will keep the Passover (Matt 26:18); Moses kept the Passover by faith (Heb 11:28); Paul hurries to keep the feast in Jerusalem (Acts 18:21).
senses.7: To commit or perpetrate a wrong — doing in the specifically negative sense of criminal or sinful action. Arabic عَمِلَ in negative contexts and Korean 저지르다 (commit a crime) mark this as morally charged. Barabbas had committed murder in the insurrection (Mark 15:7); Paul asks whether he committed a sin by preaching freely (2 Cor 11:7).
senses.8: To consider, reckon, or regard — an evaluative mental act expressed through poieo. Arabic أَجْعَلُ in its evaluative register and Korean 여기다 (regard) capture this cognitive sense. Paul does not count his life precious (Acts 20:24); he serves God in his spirit (Rom 1:9) — action as inward reckoning.
senses.9: To work or labor at a task — poieo as sustained toil rather than a discrete act. Arabic عَمِلَ (labor) and Korean 일하다 (work) distinguish this from punctual doing. The last-hired workers worked one hour yet received equal pay (Matt 20:12); adversaries were working against Paul (Acts 25:3).
senses.10: In Acts 1:1 Luke refers to his former treatise — what he 'made' or composed. This is the literary-compositional sense: to author or compile a written account. Spanish hice and German tut render it generically, but the context is clearly that of producing a literary work — the Gospel of Luke.
senses.11: In Heb 3:2 the sense is 'appoint' or 'make faithful' — God appointed Moses over his house. Spanish que hizo and the broader context of faithful service show poieo shading into divine commissioning, parallel to the appointment sense in Mark 3:14 (sense 4) but with a theologically distinct emphasis on God as the agent.

gloss_terse: Down, according to, throughout, against; a preposition of direction, standard, and distribution
gloss_readable: One of the most frequent and flexible prepositions in the Greek New Testament, kata governs either the genitive (down from, against) or the accusative (according to, throughout, each). Its root image is downward motion — a demon-possessed herd rushing down a cliff (Matt 8:32) — but this spatial seed blossoms into a rich array of relational meanings. With the accusative it expresses conformity to a standard (kata ton nomon), distribution across individuals or times (kath' hemeran, daily), and spatial extent (throughout Judea). The multilingual evidence is telling: where Greek uses one preposition, Arabic deploys حَسَبَ, عَبْرَ, ضِدَّ, and others, revealing how much semantic work kata performs.

senses.1: The overwhelmingly dominant sense: conformity to a norm, standard, or pattern. With 332 occurrences, kata + accusative expresses 'according to' — Arabic حَسَبَ/وَفْقًا, Korean 따라, Spanish según. Central to Pauline theology: kata ton nomon (according to the law), kata sarka (according to the flesh), kata Christon (according to Christ). Matt 16:27 and Matt 25:15 show judgment and distribution according to standard.
senses.2: Distributive kata: 'each, every, one by one.' Korean 매/각각 and Spanish cada capture the itemizing function. Kath' hemeran means 'daily' (Luke 9:23); kath' hena means 'one by one' (Mark 14:19); kat' oikon means 'house by house' (Acts 2:46). A grammaticalized function quite distant from the spatial root.
senses.3: Spatial extension: 'throughout, along, across' a region. Arabic عَبْرَ (across) and Spanish a lo largo de (along) capture the distributive-spatial sense. Used for the spread of Jesus's fame throughout Galilee (Luke 4:14), famine throughout the land (Luke 15:14), and earthquakes in various places (Matt 24:7).
senses.4: Locative: 'at, in, among' — marking a specific place without implying motion through it. Arabic فِي (in) and Korean 에서 (at/in) reflect static position. Dreams and visions occur kata + place: the angel appears kat' onar (in a dream, Matt 1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22). A crucial locative frozen in Matthean dream formulae.
senses.5: Instrumental or manner: 'by, through, in the manner of.' Arabic بِـ (by means of) captures this attendant-circumstance usage. Kat' idian overlaps with sense 7, but broader instrumental uses include kata sarka (by fleshly means) and kata panta tropon (in every way). Mark 1:27 — a new teaching with authority, by/according to something unprecedented.
senses.6: Directional: 'toward, before, facing.' Arabic نَحْوَ (toward) and Spanish hacia distinguish this from static location. Kata prosopon means 'before the face of' (Luke 2:31; Acts 3:13). The road going down kata from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:26) preserves the original downward directional sense in a geographic context.
senses.7: The frozen phrase kat' idian: 'privately, alone, apart.' Korean 따로 (separately) and Spanish a solas (alone) show consistent cross-linguistic specificity. Jesus withdraws kat' idian to pray (Matt 14:13, 23), teaches his disciples privately (Matt 17:1, 19; Mark 4:34). A lexicalized idiom with its own entry in most grammars.
senses.8: Topical: 'concerning, about, with respect to.' Arabic بِشَأْنِ (concerning) and Korean 에 관하여 (regarding) mark this as discourse-reference rather than standard-conformity. Ta kata eme means 'my affairs/circumstances' (Eph 6:21; Phil 1:12). Felix defers the case, being more accurately informed about the Way (Acts 24:22).
senses.9: The original spatial root: 'down, down from' with the genitive. Preserved in vivid narrative: the swine rushed kata tou kremnou (down the cliff) into the sea (Matt 8:32; Mark 5:13; Luke 8:33). Also in 1 Cor 11:4 — praying with something down over the head. The concrete image from which all metaphorical senses derive.
senses.10: Exceeding measure: 'beyond, surpassingly.' Greek kath' hyperbolen (beyond measure) is nearly a fixed adverbial phrase. Arabic فَوْقَ الْحَدّ and Korean 극도로 (extremely) confirm the superlative force. Paul was persecuting the church kath' hyperbolen (Gal 1:13); affliction was kath' hyperbolen beyond strength (2 Cor 1:8; 4:17).
senses.11: Hostile opposition: 'against' with the genitive. Arabic ضِدَّ (against) and Spanish contra isolate this adversarial sense. A tempestuous wind called Euraquilo beat kata of the ship (Acts 27:14); the Lord comes to execute judgment against (kata) the ungodly (Jude 1:15). The genitive construction marks personal or impersonal opposition.

gloss_terse: Be full, fill, fulfill; also complete a period, set gems, satisfy appetite, or fully follow
gloss_readable: A foundational Hebrew verb whose physical image — a container brimming to capacity — extends into some of Scripture's most significant theological concepts. In the Qal stative, the earth is full of violence (Gen 6:13) or the temple full of glory (2 Chr 5:13). In the Piel causative, God commands humanity to fill the earth (Gen 1:28), and artisans fill stone settings with gems (Exod 31:5). The fulfillment sense bridges concrete and abstract: days are filled to completion (Gen 25:24), promises are filled to fruition, and Caleb 'fills after' the Lord in wholehearted devotion (Num 14:24). Arabic distinguishes مَلَأَ (fill, transitive) from مَلُؤَ (be full, intransitive), preserving the same Qal/Piel polarity found in Hebrew.

senses.1: Piel causative: actively filling a vessel, space, or person. Arabic مَلَأَ/يَمْلَأُ, Korean 채우다, and Swahili -jaza all deploy transitive 'fill' verbs. The dominant active sense across 90 occurrences: God fills the earth with creatures (Gen 1:22, 28), Rebekah fills her jar (Gen 24:16), the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle (Exod 40:34–35).
senses.2: Qal stative: to be full, describing a state of fullness without active agency. Arabic مَلِيء (full) and Korean 가득하다 (be brimming) capture the adjectival quality. The earth is full of violence (Gen 6:13), the Jordan is full to overflowing at harvest (Josh 3:15), the house is full of people (Judg 16:27).
senses.3: To fulfill, complete, or bring to full measure — the temporal-purposive extension of physical filling. Arabic أَتَمَّ/تَمَّ (complete), Korean 이루다/성취하다, and Swahili -timiza (fulfill) confirm this distinct semantic register. Days of pregnancy are fulfilled (Gen 25:24), a week of wedding celebration is completed (Gen 29:27–28), and days of embalming are fulfilled (Gen 50:3).
senses.4: Niphal: to become filled or be filled passively — the earth becomes filled with violence (Gen 6:11), Egypt swarms and becomes filled with frogs (Exod 8:21), the Nile becomes filled with blood. Arabic امتلأ (Form VIII reflexive-passive) and Korean 채워지다 (be filled) capture the middle-passive voice. Forty-two occurrences mark this as a major pattern.
senses.5: Qal used transitively rather than statively — an older or variant usage where the Qal itself carries active force. Arabic مَلَأَ/مَلَأُوا and Korean 채우다 match the transitive frame. 'Consecrate yourselves' in Exod 32:29 is literally 'fill your hands'; Elijah commands 'fill four jars with water' (1 Kgs 18:34). Thirteen occurrences preserve this archaic transitive Qal.
senses.6: The idiom mille acharei YHWH: 'to fill after the LORD,' meaning to follow fully or be wholly devoted. Arabic اتَّبَعَ (follow) and Korean 충실히 따르다 (follow faithfully) show cross-linguistic specificity. Said uniquely of Caleb (Num 14:24; 32:11–12; Deut 1:36) and negatively of Solomon who did not fully follow the LORD (1 Kgs 11:6). A theologically rich idiom.
senses.7: Piel/Pual specialized craft sense: to set or inlay precious stones into a mounting. Arabic رَصَّعَ (inset gems), Korean 박다 (embed), and the Exodus craftsmanship context confirm this technical meaning. Bezalel is gifted in setting stones (Exod 31:5; 35:33); the beloved's hands are set with jewels (Song 5:14).
senses.8: Piel extended to satisfying appetite or desire — filling hunger rather than a vessel. Arabic يُشْبِعُ (satisfy, satiate) and Korean 채우다 with appetite collocations distinguish this from generic filling. Can you satisfy the appetite of young lions? (Job 38:39); a thief steals to satisfy his hunger (Prov 6:30).
senses.9: In Job 20:22, 'in the fullness of his sufficiency' — a nominal or stative use describing the peak or plenitude of abundance. Spanish en la plenitud de captures the abstract-noun quality. The verse warns that distress comes precisely when one's abundance is at its fullest, an ironic reversal of the root's positive connotation.
senses.10: In Jer 4:5, an adverbial use meaning 'fully, with full voice' — cry out male', fill the proclamation. Spanish a plena voz (at full voice) and the context of urgent prophetic warning confirm this as an intensifying adverb derived from the root sense of completeness.
senses.11: In Job 16:10, a difficult form where 'they fill/gather themselves' against Job — likely meaning they mass together or assemble in hostile fullness. Spanish se llenan and the parallelism with striking and reproach suggest a crowd filling up against the sufferer. A rare adversarial extension of the filling image.
